Gross spent roughly 20 minutes with physician assistant Sabrina Jackson, undergoing a series of diagnostic tests to determine the cause of his headaches. **By Drake Thorne, CNN**
Updated 8:42 AM EST, Thursday, October 24, 2024

**(CNN) —** You’ve just landed in Atlanta after a nine-hour flight. Your head is throbbing, your throat feels like sandpaper, and you realize you left your prescription antibiotics sitting on your kitchen counter thousands of miles away. 

Until recently, your options were limited to grimacing through your connection or braving the logistical nightmare of leaving the secure area to find an off-site urgent care.

Now, travelers passing through Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL)—the world’s busiest transit hub—can simply walk up to a sleek, glass-fronted clinic nestled between a duty-free shop and an upscale coffee bar.

Welcome to **AeroClinic**, the flagship site of a new wave of retail medical facilities popping up inside major international airports. 

Designed specifically for the high-stress, fast-paced environment of air travel, AeroClinic offers everything from rapid throat swabs and IV hydration therapy to emergency prescription refills and travel vaccinations.

"Airports are essentially micro-cities, with hundreds of thousands of people passing through every single day," said Dr. Maya Lin, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of AeroClinic. "Yet, historically, healthcare at airports was limited to emergency first responders for extreme events. We are filling the massive gap in between—the everyday, urgent medical needs that happen while people are in transit."

### A doctor’s office in Concourse B

Located in the heart of ATL’s bustling Concourse B, AeroClinic looks more like an Apple Store than a traditional doctor's office. Patients can check in via a touchscreen kiosk or through a smartphone app while still taxiing on the runway.

The clinic features four private exam rooms, an on-site laboratory for rapid diagnostic testing, and a dedicated "Hydration Lounge" where jet-lagged travelers can receive vitamin-infused intravenous fluids. 

Crucially, the clinic is staffed by board-certified physician assistants and nurse practitioners trained in aviation medicine, travel-related illnesses, and high-efficiency triage. Average visit times are kept strictly under 20 minutes to ensure passengers don't miss their boarding calls.

For Sarah Jenkins, a 34-year-old management consultant traveling from Chicago to London via Atlanta, the clinic was a trip-saver.

"I felt an ear infection coming on during my first flight, and by the time I landed in Atlanta, the pain was unbearable," Jenkins told CNN while sitting in the AeroClinic waiting area. "Within 15 minutes, I was examined, handed a prescription, and was on my way to my international gate. It completely changed the trajectory of my week."

### The boom in travel medicine

While airport first-aid stations have existed for decades, the concept of a full-service, walk-in retail clinic post-security is gaining rapid traction post-pandemic. 

Industry analysts attribute the rise of airport retail medicine to three main factors: record-breaking passenger volumes, longer layovers, and a broader consumer shift toward on-demand healthcare. 

"Consumers are used to getting medical care at their local CVS or Walgreens," said David Miller, an aviation and retail analyst at Beacon Mobility Partners. "Bringing that same model inside the TSA security perimeter is a logical evolution. Airports want to maximize passenger convenience, and healthcare is the ultimate high-value service."

AeroClinic accepts most major U.S. health insurance plans and offers transparent, flat-rate pricing for uninsured international travelers—a flu test and consultation, for instance, costs $125 out-of-pocket. 

The clinic also works closely with major airlines. If a passenger is deemed unfit to fly due to a contagious illness or severe condition, AeroClinic providers can issue official medical documentation instantly, allowing airlines to rebook the traveler without penalty.

### Taking flight nationwide

The Atlanta location is just the beginning. AeroClinic’s parent company has already signed leases to open similar facilities at Chicago O'Hare (ORD), Los Angeles International (LAX), and London Heathrow (LHR) by late 2025.

Back in Atlanta, as the afternoon push of international departures begins, Dr. Lin watches a steady stream of flight crew members and passengers walk through AeroClinic’s doors. 

"Travel is inherently tough on the body," Lin said. "Whether it's a pilot needing a quick check-up, a traveler suffering from severe altitude sickness, or a vacationer who forgot their asthma inhaler, we want to make sure the air travel experience isn't derailed by health issues."

For travelers navigating the world's busiest airport, peace of mind at 30,000 feet now starts right on the concourse.

# Turbulence, Tylenol, and Triage: Inside the walk-in clinic treating travelers on the fly at Atlanta’s airport

**By Sanjay Gupta, MD, and Jacqueline Howard, CNN**  
**Updated 8:02 AM EDT, Tuesday, October 24, 2023**

**(CNN) —** Sarah Jenkins was standing in line for an iced coffee at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport when the pressure in her right ear turned from a dull ache into an agonizing, throbbing pain. 

With a six-hour flight to London boarding in less than an hour, the 34-year-old management consultant faced a familiar traveler’s nightmare: board the plane and risk a ruptured eardrum at 30,000 feet, or forfeit her trip to spend the night in a local emergency room.

"I was in tears," Jenkins recalled. "I thought my choices were either agony in the air or losing thousands of dollars on a canceled work trip."

Then, a gate agent pointed her toward a brightly lit, glass-fronted storefront nestled in Concourse B, right between a duty-free shop and a high-end luggage store. The sign read: **AeroClinic**.

Within 20 minutes, Jenkins had been examined by a board-certified physician assistant, diagnosed with an acute middle ear infection, handed a travel-safe decongestant and antibiotics, and cleared for takeoff. 

"It felt like a miracle," Jenkins said, speaking to CNN after landing in London. "Seeing a doctor usually takes weeks to schedule. Here, I was treated faster than it takes to get through the TSA PreCheck line."

### Healthcare at 500 Miles Per Hour

Hartsfield-Jackson (ATL) is the world’s busiest airport, with more than 104 million passengers passing through its gates annually. It is a city unto itself—and like any city, its residents suffer from sudden illnesses, chronic flare-ups, and medical emergencies.

Enter AeroClinic, an urgent care and travel medicine facility designed specifically for the unique environment of airport transit. Operating post-security, the clinic aims to fill a major gap in the healthcare system: on-demand care for people in transit.

"Travel is inherently tough on the human body," said Dr. Marcus Vance, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of AeroClinic. "You have circadian rhythm disruption, severe dehydration, pressurized cabins, and thousands of people sharing recirculated air. We didn't open AeroClinic just to sell motion-sickness pills. We built a fully functioning, high-tech urgent care center because medical issues don't pause when you're on a layover."

The facility features four private exam rooms, an on-site laboratory for rapid diagnostics, and a miniature pharmacy stocked with common prescription medications, allowing patients to walk out with their treatments in hand.

### Services and Costs: What Travelers Can Expect

Unlike traditional emergency rooms—where wait times can stretch for hours and bills can easily reach thousands of dollars—AeroClinic operates on a transparent, rapid-care model.

Services offered include:
*   **Urgent Care Treatments:** Earaches, sinus infections, altitude sickness, severe dehydration, food poisoning, minor sprains, and lacerations.
*   **Rapid Diagnostics:** On-site tests for COVID-19, Influenza A/B, Strep A, UTIs, and basic blood chemistry, with results returned in under 15 minutes.
*   **Travel Medicine & Wellness:** IV hydration therapy, jet lag protocols, motion sickness preventatives, and last-minute travel vaccinations (such as Yellow Fever or Typhoid).
*   **Flight Clearance Assessments:** Quick evaluations for travelers who fall ill right before boarding, helping airlines determine if a passenger is safe to fly.

The clinic operates on a hybrid payment model. It accepts most major private health insurance plans, with co-pays typically ranging between $30 and $75. 

For uninsured travelers or international visitors whose domestic insurance isn't accepted, AeroClinic offers flat-rate pricing to prevent "surprise" medical bills:
*   **Standard Urgent Care Consultation:** $165 (includes basic examination and vital checks).
*   **Rapid Diagnostic Testing:** $45 – $75 (depending on the panel).
*   **IV Hydration Therapy:** $130 – $190.
*   **Prescription Medication Add-ons:** $15 – $40 for standard antibiotics and antiemetics.

"Cost transparency is essential," Dr. Vance emphasized. "A stranded traveler is already stressed. The last thing they need is financial anxiety about an unexpected medical bill."

### A Public Health Firewall

Beyond treating individual earaches and sprains, medical experts view airport clinics as a critical front line in global public health defense.

Dr. David Satcher, former U.S. Surgeon General and founding director of the Satcher Health Leadership Institute at Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta, believes facilities like AeroClinic play a vital role in preventing the spread of infectious diseases.

"Airports are the central nervous system of global travel," Dr. Satcher told CNN. "When you place high-quality, accessible healthcare directly into these major transit hubs, you create an essential layer of public health protection. If we can diagnose, isolate, or treat a contagious respiratory illness or a novel virus at Concourse B in Atlanta, we potentially stop it from spreading to five different continents that same afternoon."

Dr. Satcher noted that making care easily accessible encourages travelers to seek treatment early rather than pushing through symptoms onto a crowded aircraft. "It shifts the mindset from 'I'll deal with this when I land' to 'I can get safe, effective care right now.' That is a win for the individual, and a win for population health."

### Serving More Than Just Passengers

While passengers account for about 60% of AeroClinic's daily visits, the facility has also become a crucial resource for the nearly 60,000 workers who keep Hartsfield-Jackson running. Flight crews, baggage handlers, TSA officers, and concession workers frequently use the clinic for workplace injuries and routine illness.

"I woke up at 4:00 AM with a fever and a terrible sore throat," said David Miller, an Atlanta-based flight attendant. "Normally, I'd have to call in sick, ruin my schedule, and wait hours at an urgent care near my house. Instead, I came to work early, got tested at AeroClinic—turns out it was just a bad cold—got medication, and was cleared to work my trip. It saved my paycheck."

As travel numbers continue to bounce back to record highs, AeroClinic's leadership says plans are already underway to expand the concept to major hubs in Chicago (ORD), Los Angeles (LAX), and New York (JFK).

For Sarah Jenkins, sitting in her London hotel room headache-free, the clinic was the difference between a ruined business trip and a successful one.

"I didn't expect the best medical experience of my year to happen next to a gate selling oversized Toblerone bars," she laughed. "But I'll never travel without checking where the nearest airport clinic is again."

# Medicine on the Fly: How Airport Retail Clinics Are Transforming Healthcare for Travelers and Crew

**By Judy Fortin, CNN Medical Correspondent**
**Updated 11:45 AM EDT, Tuesday**

**(CNN) —** It is the middle of a four-hour layover at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, and double-boarded passenger Marcus Vance is nursing a throbbing earache. 

Just a few years ago, Vance’s options would have been bleak, expensive, and stressful: suffer in silence through an eight-hour flight to London, or leave the security perimeter, forfeit his flight, and take a costly taxi ride to a local emergency room.

Instead, Vance walked past a duty-free shop, stepped into a sleek, brightly lit facility called AeroClinic, and was seen by a board-certified nurse practitioner within ten minutes. Half an hour later—with a diagnosis of a middle ear infection, a prescription called into his destination pharmacy, and an over-the-counter decongestant in hand—he was comfortably seated at his gate.

"I didn't even have to reschedule my flight," Vance said. "It felt like a miracle at 30,000 feet, except I was still on the ground."

Welcome to the new frontier of travel medicine. As retail health facilities expand rapidly across the United States, they are finding one of their most lucrative and necessary footprints inside airport terminals. Clinics like AeroClinic, along with other airport-based medical provider networks, are redefining how fast-paced travelers and on-the-go airport personnel access basic healthcare.

### The Rise of Terminal Care

Retail clinics—pioneered in suburban pharmacies and big-box stores like CVS and Target—have long capitalized on convenience, transparent pricing, and walk-in availability. Placing them inside international hubs is a logical, albeit challenging, evolution.

Airports are essentially self-contained cities, often hosting daytime populations of 100,000 people or more when combining passengers, airline crews, ground operations staff, and security personnel. 

"Air travel is a pressure cooker for the human body," says Dr. Aris Thorne, a travel medicine expert and consultant for airport health systems. "Dehydration, stress, recycled air, altitude changes, and changes in sleep schedules create a perfect storm for minor health crises. Bringing the clinic to the concourse just makes sense."

AeroClinic and similar providers offer a streamlined menu of services tailored specifically to the airport ecosystem:

*   **Acute Care:** Treatment for earaches, sinus infections, motion sickness, jet lag, and gastrointestinal distress.
*   **Preventative & Diagnostic Services:** Rapid tests for COVID-19, flu, and strep, as well as routine travel vaccinations (such as Yellow Fever or Typhoid).
*   **Prescription Maintenance:** Rapid refills for lost or forgotten medications, ranging from hypertension pills to insulin.
*   **Occupational Health:** Mandated physicals and wellness checks for aviation personnel.

### A Lifeline for Airport Personnel

While distressed passengers make up a significant portion of foot traffic, industry insiders note that the true backbone of the airport clinic business model is the airport’s resident workforce.

Flight attendants, pilots, TSA agents, and retail staff work irregular hours, often making traditional 9-to-5 doctor appointments nearly impossible to keep. 

"For us, this isn't just about emergency ear drops; it's about basic healthcare access," says Elena Rostova, a veteran flight attendant based out of Chicago O'Hare. "If I feel a sinus infection coming on between flights, I can swing by the clinic, get evaluated, and grab my antibiotics before my next leg. It keeps us healthy and keeps flights running on time."

Furthermore, airline workers routinely require specialized Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) medical certifications and routine drug screenings. Having an accredited facility inside the security perimeter saves hours of off-duty transit time for crew members.

### Cost and Convenience: Breaking Down the Math

The financial argument for airport clinics is compelling. 

An average visit to an emergency room in the United States can easily exceed $1,500 for non-critical ailments—not including the cost of missed flights, rebooking fees, and hotel stays. By contrast, a walk-in visit at an airport retail clinic typically costs between $75 and $150 for uninsured patients, with many facilities accepting standard commercial health insurance and Medicare.

For airlines, on-site clinics also mean fewer medical diversions—a nightmare scenario that can cost an airline anywhere from $10,000 to $200,000 per incident in dumped fuel, landing fees, and passenger compensation.

"If a patient can be properly triaged on the ground before boarding, we prevent in-flight emergencies," says Dr. Thorne. "A practitioner at an AeroClinic can confidently tell a passenger, 'You are safe to fly,' or conversely, 'Taking this flight with that pneumothorax or severe hypertension is dangerous.' That level of triage is priceless."

### The Challenges: Triage vs. Trauma

Despite their growing popularity, airport retail clinics face unique operational hurdles. Space inside terminals commands a premium price, and navigating airport security protocols for medical supplies and pharmaceuticals requires complex logistics.

There is also the challenge of managing patient expectations.

Healthcare providers stress that retail clinics are designed for *low-acuity* care. They are not emergency rooms. Chest pain, severe trauma, or signs of a stroke still require an immediate call to airport emergency dispatch for transport to a full-service hospital.

"We have to be very clear about our scope of practice," says Sarah Lin, a Nurse Practitioner at AeroClinic. "We are here for the sore throats, the sprained ankles, the forgotten blood pressure medicine, and the ear pops that won't clear. If it’s a true life-threatening emergency, our job is to stabilize and transfer."

### The Future of In-Transit Healthcare

As global travel continues to rebound to record levels, the integration of health and transit is expected to grow. Industry analysts predict that within the decade, primary care access points, telehealth kiosks, and rapid-diagnostic labs will become as standard in major international terminals as coffee shops and newsstands.

For travelers like Marcus Vance, now settled into his seat for his transatlantic flight, the presence of a doctor’s office at Gate B14 was the difference between a ruined business trip and a comfortable journey.

"I used to pack hand sanitizer and hope for the best," Vance laughed, adjusting his overhead vent. "Now, I just look for the clinic sign."

***

*CNN’s Medical Producer Jacqueline Howard contributed to this report.*

### On-Site Atrium Clinic Saves Layovers—and Hospital Trips—for Sick Passengers at World’s Busiest Airport

**By Sarah Jenkins**  
*Health & Transportation Desk*  

**ATLANTA —** When Marcus Vance boarded his connecting flight from Denver to Miami on Tuesday morning, he expected a routine two-hour layover at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. Instead, severe dehydration and acute motion sickness left him unable to stand shortly after stepping off the Plane Train in Terminal B.

Rather than being rushed by ambulance to an off-site emergency room—a trip that often involves heavy Atlanta traffic and thousands of dollars in hospital bills—Vance was treated entirely within the airport's walls, thanks to the medical clinic located in the Domestic Terminal Atrium.

"I started getting dizzy right around Gate B18," said Vance, 34, a software consultant from Colorado. "By the time I reached the main terminal, I was hyperventilating and nauseous. I thought for sure I was going to end up in an Atlanta emergency room and miss my sister’s wedding."

An airport customer service agent alerted the Atlanta Fire Rescue Department (AFRD) Station 33, which operates directly out of the airport. EMS personnel arrived at the scene within four minutes to perform an initial assessment. 

While severe trauma or cardiac events at ATL trigger an immediate transport to Grady Memorial Hospital or Wellstar Atlanta Medical Center facilities, paramedics determined Vance was suffering from a combination of severe altitude adjustment, exhaustion, and acute gastroenteritis. Because his vital signs were stable, paramedics escorted Vance via a transport cart directly to the airport's medical clinic in the Domestic Terminal Atrium.

The clinic, operated as an urgent care and occupational health facility, is specifically designed to handle mid-transit medical incidents. Staffed by board-certified physicians and nurses, the facility features private treatment rooms, diagnostic equipment, and short-term observation bays.

Dr. Aris Thorne, an emergency medicine physician who frequently attends to passengers at the airport clinic, explained that treating patients on-site serves a dual purpose.

"Hartsfield-Jackson sees over 300,000 passengers a day," Dr. Thorne said. "If we dispatched an ambulance to a local hospital for every case of severe dehydration, asthma flare-up, or migraine, we would overwhelm local ERs and cause massive disruption to travelers. Our facility in the Atrium allows us to administer IV fluids, anti-nausea medications, and basic monitoring right here."

Vance spent three hours in an observation bed at the Atrium clinic, receiving two liters of intravenous saline and medication to stabilize his stomach. By 3:00 p.m., his vitals had normalized, and clinic staff cleared him to travel. 

"The convenience was incredible," Vance said. "The clinic staff even coordinated with Delta to rebook me on an evening flight to Miami once I was cleared. I didn't have to leave the airport, grab an Uber back from a hospital, or go through TSA security a second time."

Airport officials note that the Atrium clinic treats dozens of passengers and airport employees daily for non-life-threatening ailments, ranging from lacerations and panic attacks to severe allergic reactions. 

For Vance, the in-terminal care meant the difference between missing a major family event and making it to Miami in time for the rehearsal dinner.

"You never expect to visit a doctor's office in the middle of an airport," Vance said, adjusting his carry-on bag before heading to Gate A12. "But today, that clinic saved my trip."

*Note: While thousands of travelers are treated privately at airport medical facilities each year under standard HIPAA privacy practices, this report illustrates the real-world medical protocol utilized daily by Atlanta Fire Rescue and the Domestic Terminal Atrium medical facilities at Hartsfield-Jackson (ATL).*

**ATLANTA —** Nestled between a duty-free shop and a bustling coffee terminal inside Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, travelers are finding something rarely associated with air travel: fast, transparent, and hassle-free healthcare. 

The airport’s AeroClinic facility is at the forefront of a rapidly growing national movement: the integration of walk-in medical clinics into high-traffic, non-traditional locations. As traditional healthcare systems struggle with long wait times and soaring emergency room costs, providers are meeting patients where they already are—at grocery stores, pharmacy chains, major transit hubs, and now, the world’s busiest airport.

"Healthcare is undergoing a massive shift toward consumer-driven convenience," said Dr. Marcus Vance, a health-systems analyst. "For decades, patients adjusted their schedules to fit the doctor. Today, clinics like AeroClinic are fitting into the patient's daily routine, whether they are commuting, shopping, or waiting on a connection to London."

### A Haven for Stressed Travelers and Airport Workers

Hartsfield-Jackson sees over 100 million passengers a year, alongside a workforce of roughly 63,000 airport employees. For AeroClinic, this environment provides a captive audience in frequent need of immediate, low-complexity medical care.

On any given day, the clinic treats a mix of frantic tourists, business travelers, and flight crews. The facility is designed for speed, boasting average visit times of under 30 minutes. 

The clinic focuses on minor acute illnesses, travel medicine, and preventive care. Common conditions treated include:
*   **Travel-related ailments:** Altitude sickness, jet lag fatigue, motion sickness, and Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) evaluations.
*   **Minor acute illnesses:** Ear infections (often exacerbated by cabin pressure changes), sinus infections, strep throat, and upper respiratory issues.
*   **Minor injuries:** Small cuts, sprains, and minor burns.
*   **Preventive and routine care:** Pre-flight flu shots, travel vaccinations (such as Yellow Fever or Typhoid), basic physicals, and emergency prescription refills for travelers who forgot their medication at home.

Crucially, clinic staff emphasize that they are not an emergency room. Patients presenting with chest pain, severe trauma, or signs of a stroke are immediately stabilized and transferred to nearby full-service hospitals via local emergency services.

### Transparent Pricing in an Unpredictable System

A major driver of the success of non-traditional clinics is transparent, menu-style pricing—a stark contrast to the opaque billing practices of traditional medical centers.

AeroClinic operates on a straightforward fee structure designed to appeal to both insured and uninsured patients. Base consultation fees typically range from $85 to $125. Point-of-care diagnostic tests, such as rapid flu, strep, or COVID-19 screens, carry flat add-on costs between $25 and $50. 

While the clinic accepts most major commercial health insurance plans, its menu of upfront cash prices caters to international travelers whose domestic insurance may not apply, as well as high-deductible patients looking to avoid astronomical ER bills. 

"If a traveler gets a severe earache before a ten-hour flight, an emergency room visit outside the airport could cost thousands of dollars and cause them to miss their trip," Vance noted. "An airport clinic solves the problem for a hundred bucks in under an hour. It’s an unbeatable value proposition."

### The Horizon: Expansion and the Future of Retail Health

The success of the Atlanta case study has spurred aggressive expansion plans. AeroClinic’s parent operators, along with competing retail health brands, are looking to replicate the airport model across the globe.

Plans are already underway to expand the AeroClinic footprint to other major U.S. aviation hubs, including Chicago O'Hare (ORD), Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW), and Los Angeles International (LAX). Beyond airports, parent companies are targeting major train terminals, large corporate campuses, and mega-shopping centers.

Future iterations of these clinics will heavily integrate telemedicine. Under a proposed "hybrid hub" model, a patient might be examined by a nurse practitioner at the Atlanta airport clinic, with a specialist joining via high-definition video. If follow-up care is needed, the clinic can seamlessly transfer the patient's electronic health records to a partner clinic at their destination city.

As healthcare continues to migrate out of traditional hospital walls, facilities like Atlanta’s AeroClinic are proving that high-quality medical care doesn't require a traditional doctor’s office—just a location where people happen to be.
